zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical aid: the supplied Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0 (https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). This review supplies its own scan-based transcription decisions and English notes; the index is not a diplomatic authority.

runs.text: Carta em que ſe manda chamar a al-

lines.note: Meshibu is a written summons: a letter ordering someone to be called. The divided alguem continues on the next physical line.
Guem completes alguem. Meshibu wo nasaruru gives the honorific issuing of the summons; Dar o leads into the lord as subject below.

runs.text: ſenhor carta, ou patente pera chamar alguem.

lines.note: The lord gives a letter or patent to summon someone. Patente is a formal authorization here, not a Japanese headword.
Meshikaye is changing or exchanging; ishoo wo introduces clothing as its object. The visible long-o mark is a caron.
Meshikayuru completes the example of changing clothes. Voco- begins the honorific word for a palanquin in the next example.
Vokoshi wo meshikayuru means transferring between palanquins. The Portuguese construction continues with the destination and the noble passenger below.

The person transferring to another palanquin is explicitly noble. No secure grave is visible over the o of peſſoa; the OCR accent is removed. The tiny mark over the initial preposition is inconclusive, so the baseline a is retained.
Meshikayeshi is giving back or restoring; restituir is physically divided. The printed principal part ita is retained, not replaced with the ending expected from a modern verb paradigm.
Honryoo wo ba meshikayesareta describes the restoration of an original holding or income. The honorific verb agrees with the restitution gloss; tuir finishes restituir.

The Portuguese says that his estate or revenue was returned. Xid. is the upright citation label. The scan has one italic Tornoulhe, not the duplicated OCR T; the embedded Japanese Riǒchi remains in the locally printed italic type.
A second sense is calling someone again. This is a continuation of meshikayeshi rather than another independent lemma.
Meshikome is keeping someone imprisoned or confined. The alternative description beginning ou is completed in the following two rows.

runs.text: cercado em algum lugar de maneira que não

lines.note: The confinement is in a place arranged so that the person cannot leave. The negative não belongs to the verb on the following line.
Saya fora completes the clause 'does not go out'. The historical spelling saya is preserved instead of modern saia.
Meshihanashi means taking away or removing. Its printed aita principal part is historical morphology, not an omitted shi to be supplied.
Chigyoo wo meshi hanasareta concerns removal of a revenue holding. The Portuguese Tirou- continues into lhe below, while the Japanese keeps its printed internal space.

runs.text: lhe arenda, ou foilhe tirada arenda.

lines.note: The gloss permits both 'he took away his income' and 'his income was taken away'. Initial lhe, rather than OCR the, completes Tirou-lhe across the physical break.
Meshigushi is taking someone along. The supplied suru and ita are the dictionary's principal-form endings, not Portuguese words.

Meshii is losing sight; the Portuguese says the eyes become blind and labels the verb defective. Preserve the unusual printed abbreviated forms jta and ijte rather than reconstructing a modern paradigm.
Meshiidasare is honorifically summoning. Ya- begins yado no in the example, so this row must remain connected with the householder below.
Yado no tayuu wo meshiidasarete is rendered as summoning the master of the house outside. The scan supports Tayǔuo, not OCR Tayôuo; Cha- starts chamando.

runs.text: mando pera fora aodono da caſa. ¶ Item,

lines.note: Mando completes chamando, calling the householder outside. A second sense begins after Item and is explained on the next row.

runs.text: Pedir, ou fazer vir diante. Vt,

lines.note: The second sense is requesting something or having it brought before one. Katana wo supplies the sword as object of that action.
The sword is brought forward and inspected, with honorific wording in both Japanese verbs. Fazendo introduces the corresponding Portuguese construction continued below.
The continuation completes 'having the sword brought and looking at it'. Catana is the Japanese weapon name embedded in an otherwise Portuguese explanation; its printed italic type is retained.
Meshiidashi first refers back to the preceding sense, then introduces the lord's giving of a drinking cup. The aita ending is retained as historical inflection.

runs.text: o ſenhor, ou peßoa nobre a outros inferiores o

lines.note: The donor is a lord or noble person, the recipients his inferiors. Final o is the article for the cup named on the next line.

runs.text: Sacãzuqui fazendo os beber diante de ſi.

lines.note: The cup is offered so that the recipients drink before the lord. The marked Japanese cup-name is embedded in the Portuguese sentence; its unusual spelling is not normalized to the form on the next row.

runs.text: O dar eſte Sacazzuqui deſta ma-

lines.note: The noun meshi idashi denotes this manner of presenting the sake cup. Sacazzuqui has the visible doubled z spelling here, unlike the preceding occurrence; ma- begins maneira.
Neira completes maneira. Meshi idashi ga aru means that such an offering or drinking occasion takes place; the Portuguese continues its alternative paraphrase below.
The lord gives this drink or drinking entertainment. Beberete is the historical diminutive in the gloss, not a malformed Japanese word.
Meshi imashime means arresting or keeping someone under restraint. The object introduced by a continues on the next row.
Alguem de cerco completes the description of keeping a person surrounded or confined. It belongs to meshi imashime, not to the following upward-summoning verb.
Meshinobose means causing someone to go up by summoning them. Fazer governs sobir on the following physical line.
The destination is Miyako, the capital. The historical Portuguese verb sobir is preserved, and Miaco is an embedded Japanese place-name eligible for whole-word typeface review.

runs.text: Officio de notar, ou vigiar ſobre as

lines.note: Meshiro is defined as the office or duty of observing and watching over entrusted matters. The final article as anticipates cousas below.
The matters are those entrusted to the officeholder. The abbreviation q̃ is retained as printed rather than expanded to que.
Meshitsukai, meshitsukoo, meshitsukoota means employing someone in one's service. Both supplied vowel marks are downward carons in this impression.
Hito wo meshitsukoo illustrates employing a person. The next example begins higoro me-, with meshi divided across this and the following row.
Higoro meshitsukoota hikan is a retainer one has long employed. The Portuguese hum, not OCR bum, is supported by the local type and begins the relative clause completed below.
Servio muito tempo completes the description of a servant used for a long time. The brief line is a genuine continuation and is indented in the scan.

runs.text: Vaſo em que vem arroz cozido

lines.note: Meshitsugi is a vessel bringing cooked rice to replenish the meal. The damaged e at the beginning of the headword remains compatible with that reading; no modern spelling is substituted.

runs.text: pera refazer o que ſe come na meſa.

lines.note: The vessel supplies replacement for the rice eaten at table. Refazer carries the replenishing sense here, not repairing an object.
Meshitsure means taking someone along. The ruru and eta principal forms are kept as the dictionary presents them.
Em companhia completes the alternative Portuguese paraphrase 'in one's company'. It is not a new entry or page furniture.
Meshitori means seizing or arresting; the following row adds binding. Preserve the abbreviated u and otta forms instead of expanding their stems.
The example concerns the Heike warriors seizing this person. Feiqe no samurai belongs to a standalone Japanese quotation, not to Japanese words embedded in a Portuguese sentence.

Meshitotte shizai ni okonawoo to yuute means arresting the person and saying they would put him to death. The final yǔte has a marked u, not OCR yǒte. Its citation and Portuguese translation continue at the top of column 2.

runs.text: Feiq. Lib. 3. Os Soldados, ou gente honrada

lines.note: The Heike citation, book 3, introduces the translation of the arrest example at the foot of column 1. Soldados and honrada replace OCR Soidados and honradal; the latter's spurious l came from the right rule.

runs.text: do Fei que prendendo a eſte, & dizendo que

lines.note: The soldiers or honorable men of the Heike seize this person and say what follows. The printed Japanese name within the Portuguese has a visible internal gap, retained as Fei que.

runs.text: o auião de condenar à morte, &c.

lines.note: They were to condemn him to death. This completes the preceding column's Japanese quotation and the Portuguese sentence, rather than forming an independent entry.
Meshioki means leaving or setting something in place. The headword begins at the column's entry margin, not at the continuation indent assigned by the OCR.
Kyoo wo tana no ue ni meshiwoite describes placing the books on a shelf. The printed Japanese uses a long-o mark, while Pondo starts its translation.

runs.text: os liuros ſobre a meſa, ou parteleiro.

lines.note: The Portuguese locates the books on a table or shelf. Preserve historical parteleiro rather than modernizing its consonant order.
Meshioroshi denotes old or previously worn garments. The relative clause identifying their former wearer follows on the next row.

runs.text: algũ ſenhor, ou peſſoa hõrada deixa ja de veſtir.

lines.note: The clothes are those a lord or honorable person no longer wears. The visible peſſoa is one word; OCR peſſo a introduced a false boundary. Both nasal abbreviations are retained.
Meshiyose means summoning someone to oneself. The printed ſuru principal part is retained even though the surrounding verbs might suggest another paradigm.
Meshuuto is a prisoner or condemned person. The marked u is important to the Japanese reading and is preserved without replacing it with a modern spelling.
Messhi means being destroyed or perishing. The doubled x represents the Japanese consonant sequence; the Portuguese reflexive ending belongs to the gloss.

runs.text: Petição que ſe apreſenta a o ſenhor quã

lines.note: Meyasu is a written petition presented to the lord. The final nasal abbreviation begins quando across the physical break; the OCR's final s is not supported by the right-edge type.

runs.text: do ſe lhe não pode falar, nem hà quem interce-

lines.note: The petition is used when one cannot speak to the lord and no intermediary is available. The separate lhe não is visible, and interce- continues into interceda below.
Da completes interceda. Meyasu wo sasaguru or aguru gives two verbs for presenting the petition; the isolated l is the alternative marker, not a Japanese syllable.
Guru completes aguru, the alternative to sasaguru. The Portuguese explicitly identifies the action as presenting this petition.
Meyoo denotes a signal or gesture made with the eye. The caron over o remains distinct from an ordinary unmarked vowel.
Mezamashii describes something astonishing. The next two indented forms give the related noun and adverb rather than additional Portuguese senses.
Mezamashisa is the nominal form, astonishment or astonishing quality, attached to the preceding adjective. Its short standalone row remains part of the body text.
Mezamashuu is the adverbial form of mezamashii. The scan's marked final u corrects the OCR i and the stale kana hint derived from it.

runs.text: Peßoa que vè bem, julga, & pe

lines.note: Mezuishoo is a discerning person who sees, judges, and penetrates matters well. The final pe begins penetra without a securely visible terminal hyphen.
Netra completes penetra, describing insight into matters. It belongs with the discerning person above rather than with the following eye-movement entry.
Mezukai is movement or use of the eyes. Mezzu- begins an example using the same noun, divided at the physical line boundary.
Mezukai ga tada mono dewa nai says that the person's eye movement is not that of an ordinary man. Moui- starts the Portuguese movimento.

runs.text: mento dos olhos não he de qualquer homem.

lines.note: The eye movement does not belong to just any ordinary person. Mento completes movimento and the negative comparison supplies the force of tada mono dewa nai.
Mezurakana is equated with mezurashii: something pleasing, novel, or rare. Apra- begins aprazivel in the next row.
Zivel completes aprazivel. The definition adds newness or rarity; the final S. is the written-register label, distinct from the italic gloss.

Mezurakani is explicitly an adverb and is equated with mezurashuu. The abbreviation Adu. is Portuguese apparatus; the Japanese synonym after i is not an embedded term to flag for whole-word font toggling.
Mezurashii is glossed as new and pleasing. The scan supports noua, not OCR nona, while preserving the historical u spelling.
Mezurashisa is the nominal derivative, novelty or rarity. It is intentionally a short indented body line without a separate Portuguese definition.
Mezurashuu is the adverbial derivative of mezurashii. Its final marked u is visible and parallels the earlier synonym and the mezamashuu form.
The enlarged initial belongs to MI, the honorific prefix mi, equated with o. The OCR detached and misread its capital M; no independent NVt entry exists. The example follows on the next genuine row.
Mite and miashi are honorific hands and feet. The Portuguese identifies their possessor on the next line; this is one physical row, not two as suggested by the overlapping OCR fragment.
The honorific hands and feet belong to an exalted or holy person. This completes the illustration of the prefix, not the following first-person sense of mi.
Mi is equated first with soregashi, 'I', and then with the body. The entry deliberately gathers distinct senses; no explanatory i is supplied where it is not printed.
Mi wo mattoo shite kimi ni tsukayeyo instructs one to serve one's lord while preserving one's person. The previously omitted pilcrow is visible at the start of the example.

runs.text: Serui a voßo ſenhor conſeruando voſſo

lines.note: Xix. is the source label for the preceding Japanese sentence. The Portuguese imperative asks the reader to serve the lord while conserving the body or life; the final object continues below.
Body or life completes the object of conservando. This short line belongs to the quoted admonition and retains its continuation indentation.
This mi is a winnowing implement: a tool for sifting rice. The Japanese paraphrase and Portuguese comparison to a joeira identify the utensil rather than the preceding sense 'body'.
The implement is used to winnow and shake the rice. The printed verb joeirão is preserved rather than normalized from modern usage.

Mi, explained by konomi, means fruit. The separate far-right damanhãa completes the following time definition, not this fruit gloss; its physical placement and opening parenthesis are retained here. On this impression the tilde is over the first of the two final a-types, so the spelling is not forced to the more common nhaã pattern.

Mi no toki is defined by the source as the time from eight to ten in the morning. The morning qualifier is displaced to the right of the preceding row; it is not silently moved into reading order. The second pass confirms the small grave above a in àte, restoring the correctly aligned baseline spelling rather than normalizing it to até or removing the accent.
Mi, miru, mita is seeing. Mirume ga yoi or warui introduces a contrast in appearance, with the second alternative beginning on the next row.

runs.text: Parecer bem, ou mal à vista, ou ſer

lines.note: Warui completes the Japanese alternative 'bad'. The gloss describes looking good or bad and then extends the contrast to one's example or edifying effect.
Good or bad edification completes the preceding gloss. The scan reads edificação, not OCR edificoção; preserve its historical moral sense rather than forcing a building-related interpretation.

runs.text: Lume, ou candea que arde diante do

lines.note: Miakashi is a light or candle burning before a sacred being. The complement is the genuine final body line below, which the provisional OCR incorrectly bundled with the catchword.

The light burns before a hotoke or kami. Both Japanese religious terms occur inside the Portuguese explanation. This recovered continuation is body text; the separate right-hand Miaca. is the catchword for the intended next leaf, whose beginning is not present in the following supplied scan.
